agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# Svgbob

Svgbob can create a nice graphical representation of your text diagrams.

Svgbob provides a CLI which takes text as an input and creates an SVG image as an output.

## Demo

[**Interactive Demo**](https://ivanceras.github.io/svgbob-editor/)

## What is Svgbob?

Svgbob is a tool that converts ASCII art text diagrams into beautiful SVG graphics. It automatically recognizes shapes, lines, arrows, and text in your ASCII art and renders them as scalable vector graphics.

## Features

- Converts ASCII art diagrams to SVG
- Supports various shapes: rectangles, circles, lines, arrows
- Handles text within diagrams
- Customizable styling via legends
- Command-line interface for easy integration
- Server mode available for REST API usage

## Usage Examples

### Basic ASCII Art to SVG

Input:
```
    +------+
    |      |
    +------+
```

### Command Line Options

The CLI tool supports various options:

- `--background <color>` - Set backdrop background color (default: white)
- `--fill-color <color>` - Set fill color for solid shapes (default: black)
- `--stroke-color <color>` - Set stroke color for lines (default: black)
- `--font-family <font>` - Set font family for text (default: arial)
- `--font-size <size>` - Set font size (default: 14)
- `--stroke-width <width>` - Set stroke width for lines (default: 2)
- `--scale <factor>` - Scale the entire SVG by this factor (default: 1)
- `-o, --output <file>` - Output file (default: STDOUT)
- `-s, --inline` - Parse an inline string

### Server Mode

Svgbob can also run as a REST API server. Send ASCII art as a POST request and receive SVG output.

## Specification

For detailed information about the diagram syntax and supported features, see the [Specification](https://ivanceras.github.io/content/Svgbob/Specification.html).

## Used By

- [google/comprehensive-rust](https://github.com/google/comprehensive-rust) via [markdown-svgbob](https://github.com/boozook/mdbook-svgbob)
- [asciidoctor](https://docs.asciidoctor.org/diagram-extension/latest/diagram_types/svgbob/)
- [discourse](https://meta.discourse.org/t/discourse-svgbob/223573)
- [typst/bob-draw](https://typst.app/universe/package/bob-draw/)
- [zola](https://zola.discourse.group/t/diagramming-tool-integrations-plantuml-svgbob-graphviz-etc/269)
- [kroki](https://kroki.io/)

==server readme==
# Svgbob Server

Svgbob Server runs svgbob as a REST API, allowing you to convert ASCII art diagrams to SVG via HTTP requests.

## Usage

Start the server on a specific port and send POST requests with your ASCII art:

```sh
curl -X POST -F 'ascii=o------>' http://localhost:3000 > output.svg
```

The server accepts ASCII art as form data and returns the rendered SVG.

    print("===")

def run(args, cwd="/workspace"):
    p=subprocess.run(["/workspace/executable"]+args, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=cwd)
    return p
def run_raw(args, cwd="/workspace"):
    p=subprocess.run(["/workspace/executable"]+args, capture_output=True, cwd=cwd)
    return p

tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
print(tmpdir)
# binary file
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "bin.bob"),"wb").write(b"\xff\xfe")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "good.bob"),"w").write("hi")
os.makedirs(os.path.join(tmpdir, "out"), exist_ok=True)

p=run(["build", "-i", f"{tmpdir}/*.bob", "-o", f"{tmpdir}/out"])

for f in os.listdir(os.path.join(tmpdir,"out")):
    print(open(os.path.join(tmpdir,"out",f)).read()[:200])

# Test with directory that has no .bob files

os.makedirs(os.path.join(tmpdir2, "out"), exist_ok=True)

print(f"no bob files => EXIT {p.returncode} OUT {repr(p.stdout[:1000])} ERR {repr(p.stderr[:1000])}")

# Test build input is file path without wildcard but with dir?
p=run(["build", "-i", f"{tmpdir}/good.bob", "-o", f"{tmpdir}/out"])
print(f"single file => EXIT {p.returncode} OUT {repr(p.stdout[:1000])}")

shutil.rmtree(tmpdir)
shutil.rmtree(tmpdir2)

import subprocess, os, tempfile, shutil, glob
def run(args, cwd="/workspace"):
    p=subprocess.run(["/workspace/executable"]+args, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=cwd)
    return p

tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
print(tmpdir)
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "a.bob"),"w").write("hi")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "b.txt"),"w").write("hello")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "c.bob"),"w").write("bye")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "d.svg"),"w").write("svgcontent")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "e"),"w").write("noext")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "f.bob.txt"),"w").write("bobtxt")

    "*.bob",
    "*.txt",
    "*.svg",
    "*",
    "*.*",
    "a.bob",
    "a.*",
    "*.bob.txt",
    "f.bob.txt",
    "e",
    "*e*",
    "a*",
    "*b*",

import subprocess, os, tempfile, shutil
def run(args, cwd="/workspace"):

    return p

tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()

open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "a.bob"),"w").write("hi")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "b.bob"),"w").write("hello")
open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "c.txt"),"w").write("txtcontent")

os.makedirs(os.path.join(tmpdir, "sub"), exist_ok=True)

# Test basename filtering: pattern "a.bob" should match all .bob if no filtering, or only a.bob if filtering
for pat in [f"{tmpdir}/a.bob", f"{tmpdir}/b.bob", f"{tmpdir}/nomatch.bob", f"{tmpdir}/a*.bob", f"{tmpdir}/b*.bob", f"{tmpdir}/z*.bob"]:

        os.remove(os.path.join(tmpdir,"out",f))

# Test -o edge cases: no -o, -o empty, -o file, -o with trailing slash, -o nonexistent nested
print("=== -o edge ===")
for out_pat in [None, "", f"{tmpdir}/out", f"{tmpdir}/out/", f"{tmpdir}/newdir", f"{tmpdir}/newdir/", f"{tmpdir}/a.bob", "/nonexistent_out", f"{tmpdir}/sub/../out"]:
    for f in os.listdir(os.path.join(tmpdir,"out")):
        try: os.remove(os.path.join(tmpdir,"out",f))
        except: pass
    # clean newdir if exists
    import pathlib
    newdir = os.path.join(tmpdir,"newdir")
    if os.path.exists(newdir):
        shutil.rmtree(newdir)
    if out_pat is None:
        args=["build", "-i", f"{tmpdir}/*.bob"]
    else:
        args=["build", "-i", f"{tmpdir}/*.bob", "-o", out_pat]
    p=run(args)
    print(f"OUTPAT {out_pat!r} => EXIT {p.returncode} OUT {repr(p.stdout[:800])} ERR {repr(p.stderr[:500])}")
    # check where files went

            if svgs:
                print(f"  {d} has {svgs}")
                for f in svgs:
                    fp=os.path.join(d,f)
                    try: os.remove(fp)
                    except: pass

shutil.rmtree(tmpdir)
